readerTitle: Why saving $500 can beat selling $1,500 more
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 식당, 구독형 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 비용 1달러 절감은 이익 1달러지만, 매출 1달러는 공헌이익률만큼만 이익이 된다. 그래서 마진이 낮을수록 절감 한 건이 큰 매출과 맞먹는다. 다만 절감에는 바닥이 있고 성장에는 천장이 없다.
misconception: 매출 1달러와 비용 절감 1달러는 이익에 똑같이 기여한다. 또는 반대로, 비용 절감이 언제나 성장보다 낫다.

factChecks.note: 식당의 '판매에 따라 늘어나는 비용 70%'에 시간제 주방 인건비를 포함한 것은 단순화를 위한 가정입니다. 실제 식당의 비용 구조는 업장마다 크게 다릅니다.

cards.title: Why saving $500 can beat selling $1,500 more
body: A neighborhood restaurant owner finds two ways to add profit. She can cut $500 a month from her bills. Or she can push for more sales.
Most owners treat a dollar saved and a dollar sold as the same thing. They aren't even close.

image.label: A coin saved on one side of a scale, a stack of sales receipts on the other
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 저울 한쪽에 동전 한 개("$1 saved"), 다른 쪽에 영수증 더미("$3.33 sold"). 저울이 균형을 이루는 모습. 배경은 따뜻한 동네 식당 주방. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: How much more would she need to sell?
body: The restaurant sells $40,000 a month. Food, drink, packaging, card fees and hourly kitchen wages take 70 cents of every dollar. Rent and salaries cost $10,000 a month whatever happens.
She can save $500 a month by renegotiating insurance and dropping an unused linen service. To earn the same extra profit from sales instead, how much more would she need to sell each month?

options.feedback: It feels even, but each sale brings its own costs. Only 30 cents of every new dollar reaches profit.
Right. $500 ÷ 30% is about $1,667 in new sales to match one $500 saving. Next card shows why.
Good instinct that sales are worth less than savings here, but that overshoots. At a 30% margin, it's closer to $1,700.

cards.title: Two roads to the same $500.
body: Her monthly profit is only $2,000. So that one $500 saving lifts profit by **25%**. Matching it with sales means growing revenue by about 4%, every month, with no extra staff or space.

breakdown.label: Cost cut
breakdown.detail: Goes straight to profit, dollar for dollar

breakdown.label: What each sale keeps
breakdown.detail: After food, packaging, fees and hourly wages

cards.title: A saved dollar is worth more sales than you think
body: A dollar cut from costs adds a full dollar to profit. A dollar of new sales adds only its **contribution margin**, the share left after the costs that come with that sale.
So one dollar saved equals *1 ÷ margin* dollars of sales. At 30%, that's $3.33. This is the honest way to compare a cost cut with a growth plan: translate both into profit before you choose.

image.label: Formula card: $1 saved equals $1 divided by margin in sales
image.brief: 깔끔한 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 "$1 saved", 가운데 등호, 오른쪽에 "$1 ÷ margin in sales". 아래에 예시 "30% margin → $3.33". 단색 배경, 숫자를 크게.

cards.title: The lower your margin, the bigger a saving looks.
body: Sales needed to match a $1 cost cut, at different contribution margins. A grocery store on thin margins and a software company on fat ones face very different math.

image.label: The lower your margin, the bigger a saving looks.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: Cuts have a floor. Growth doesn't.
body: You can only cut a cost once, and never below zero. After the waste is gone, each new cut gets harder and riskier.

Growth can repeat. New customers come back next month, and they spread rent and salaries over more sales. So the smart order is usually: cut what customers will never notice first, then put your energy into growth that keeps paying.

cards.title: The math assumes sales stay the same.
body: The $500 insurance saving is safe because no diner feels it. Shrinking portions or dropping the evening server is different. Those cuts can quietly cost sales.
At a 30% margin, losing $1,667 in sales wipes out a $500 saving. That's just four regulars who stop coming, if each spends about $100 a week. Before any cut, ask: **would a customer notice?**

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your subscription app earns $100,000 a month. Each dollar of revenue keeps 80 cents after servers and payment fees. Fixed costs are $70,000, so profit is $10,000.
Your team proposes: cancel $3,000 of unused tools, halve support hours to save $5,000, or run a $2,000 campaign expected to add $6,000 in monthly revenue. What do you do?

options.text: Halve support hours. It's the biggest saving at $5,000
options.feedback: The saving is real, but slower replies can push users to cancel. Losing just $6,250 in revenue, about 6% of it, wipes out the whole $5,000.

options.text: Cancel the unused tools and stop there. Savings are certain
options.feedback: You bank a safe $3,000. But at an 80% margin, a dollar of new revenue is worth almost as much as a dollar saved, so skipping growth leaves money behind.

options.text: Cancel the unused tools and run the campaign
options.feedback: You take the cut no customer feels (+$3,000) and add growth worth about $2,800 a month if it works ($4,800 kept minus $2,000 spent).

cards.title: Turn every idea into profit before you compare.
body: A dollar saved is worth *1 ÷ margin* dollars of sales. Thin margins make cuts powerful. Fat margins make growth almost as good. Either way, cut what customers won't feel, and grow what keeps paying.
**Try it today:** take one cost you could cut. Divide it by your margin. Is it easier to save that or to sell that much more?
